title: The development of the model of the atom

notes.definition: The model of the atom has changed over time as new experimental evidence was found: from tiny indivisible spheres, to the plum pudding model, to the nuclear model with electrons in fixed orbits, and then to a nucleus containing protons and neutrons.
explanation: Scientific models change when new experimental evidence cannot be explained by the old model. The model of the atom is a classic example. Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided into anything smaller.

The discovery of the electron (by J. J. Thomson) showed that atoms contain even smaller, negatively charged particles, so atoms could be divided. This led to the plum pudding model: the atom was a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it, like fruit in a pudding. The positive and negative charges balanced, so the atom was neutral.

The alpha particle scattering experiment (carried out by Geiger and Marsden, and explained by Rutherford) fired positively charged alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. Most alpha particles went straight through, so most of the atom must be empty space. Some were deflected, so the centre of the atom must be charged (positive, because it repelled the positive alpha particles). A very few bounced back, so the mass must be concentrated in a very small region at the centre. The plum pudding model could not explain these results, so it was replaced by the nuclear model.

Niels Bohr then adapted the nuclear model. He suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (energy levels). His theoretical calculations agreed with experimental observations, such as the particular wavelengths of light emitted by atoms, so the model was accepted.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each with the same amount of positive charge. These particles were called protons. About 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted idea, James Chadwick carried out experiments that provided evidence for neutrons in the nucleus. This explained why nuclei have more mass than their protons alone would give.
keyFacts: Before the electron was discovered, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model.
Plum pudding model: a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
Alpha scattering: most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, so the atom is mostly empty space.
Alpha scattering: some were deflected, so the centre (nucleus) is charged.
Alpha scattering: very few bounced back, so the mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
The nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Bohr suggested electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances; his calculations agreed with experiments.
Later experiments showed the positive charge of the nucleus is made of protons.
Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.

keyTerms.definition: A model of the atom as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
A model of the atom with a tiny, positively charged nucleus containing most of the mass, surrounded by electrons and mostly empty space.
An experiment in which alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil; the pattern of deflections showed that atoms have a small, massive, charged nucleus.
A positively charged particle made of two protons and two neutrons.
A simplified description used to explain observations; it is changed or replaced when new evidence does not fit it.
A particle in the nucleus with one unit of positive charge; the nuclear charge is a whole number of these.

workedExamples.title: Linking alpha scattering observations to conclusions
workedExamples.question: Give each observation from the alpha scattering experiment and the conclusion drawn from it.
steps: Most alpha particles passed straight through: most of the atom is empty space.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles: the nucleus is charged (positive, so it repels positive alpha particles).
A very small number bounced back: the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a very small nucleus.
workedExamples.answer: Empty space; charged nucleus; tiny, massive nucleus.

workedExamples.title: Why the plum pudding model failed
workedExamples.question: Explain why the plum pudding model could not explain alpha particles bouncing back from gold foil.
steps: In the plum pudding model the positive charge and mass are spread out through the whole atom.
Spread-out charge would only produce weak forces, so alpha particles would pass through with tiny deflections.
Bouncing back needs a large force from a concentrated, massive, charged region: a nucleus.
workedExamples.answer: Spread-out charge and mass could not provide a force big enough to turn alpha particles back.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the alpha particles bounced back because they hit electrons.
misconceptions.right: In fact electrons are far too light to turn an alpha particle back. Alpha particles bounced back because they were repelled by the small, massive, positive nucleus.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think most alpha particles were deflected.
misconceptions.right: In fact most went straight through. Only some were deflected and very few bounced back.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the plum pudding model was a wrong guess with no evidence.
misconceptions.right: In fact it was based on the evidence available at the time (the discovery of the electron). It was replaced when new evidence did not fit.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think neutrons were discovered at the same time as the nucleus.
misconceptions.right: In fact Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons about 20 years after the nuclear model was accepted.

realWorld: The history of the atom is used as a model case of how science works: a theory is tested, and replaced when new evidence does not fit.
Bohr's idea of electrons at fixed energy levels explains why each element gives out its own pattern of coloured light, used to identify elements in stars.
Scattering experiments like Rutherford's are still used today, at much higher energies in particle accelerators, to probe the inside of protons and neutrons.
examTips: For alpha scattering, learn three observation-conclusion pairs. Each is often worth a mark.
When comparing plum pudding and nuclear models, describe where the positive charge and mass are in each.
You do not need experimental details, but you must explain why new evidence led to a change in the model.
Get the order right: indivisible spheres, plum pudding, nuclear model, Bohr's orbits, protons, Chadwick's neutrons.
summary: Atoms were first thought to be indivisible spheres.
The electron's discovery led to the plum pudding model.
Alpha scattering showed a tiny, massive, positive nucleus, so the nuclear model replaced plum pudding.
Bohr put electrons in orbits at specific distances; his calculations matched experiments.
Protons were identified as the units of positive charge; Chadwick later found evidence for neutrons.
Models change when new evidence cannot be explained.

questions.question: Before the electron was discovered, what did scientists think atoms were?
options: Balls of positive charge with electrons in them
Tiny spheres that could not be divided
A nucleus with electrons orbiting it
markScheme: 1 mark: Tiny spheres that could not be divided
questions.explanation: Before electrons were known, atoms were thought to be the smallest possible particles: tiny indivisible spheres.

questions.question: Which model describes the atom as a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it?
markScheme: 1 mark: The plum pudding model
questions.explanation: That is the plum pudding model, proposed after the electron was discovered. The nuclear model has a tiny central nucleus.

questions.question: In the alpha scattering experiment, what happened to most of the alpha particles?
options: They were absorbed by the foil
They were deflected through large angles
They passed straight through the foil
markScheme: 1 mark: They passed straight through the foil
questions.explanation: Most passed straight through, which showed that the atom is mostly empty space.

questions.question: What did the alpha particles that bounced back from the gold foil show?
options: The mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: The mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny nucleus
questions.explanation: Only something very small, massive and charged could turn an alpha particle back. Empty space is shown by particles passing straight through.

questions.question: What did Niels Bohr add to the nuclear model?
options: Electrons orbiting the nucleus at specific distances
markScheme: 1 mark: Electrons orbiting the nucleus at specific distances
questions.explanation: Bohr suggested electrons orbit at specific distances. The nucleus came from alpha scattering, and neutrons from Chadwick.

questions.question: Which scientist provided the experimental evidence for the existence of neutrons?
markScheme: 1 mark: James Chadwick
questions.explanation: James Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons, about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.

questions.question: Why was the plum pudding model replaced by the nuclear model?
options: New experimental evidence could not be explained by the plum pudding model
markScheme: 1 mark: New experimental evidence could not be explained by the plum pudding model
questions.explanation: Models are replaced when new evidence does not fit. The alpha scattering results could not be explained by spread-out positive charge.

questions.question: Which is the correct order in which these ideas were developed?
options: Plum pudding, indivisible spheres, nuclear model, neutrons
Indivisible spheres, nuclear model, plum pudding, neutrons
Indivisible spheres, plum pudding, nuclear model, neutrons
Nuclear model, plum pudding, indivisible spheres, neutrons
markScheme: 1 mark: Indivisible spheres, plum pudding, nuclear model, neutrons
questions.explanation: Atoms were spheres first, then plum pudding after the electron, then the nuclear model after alpha scattering, and neutrons last (Chadwick).

questions.question: Some alpha particles were deflected by the gold foil. Which conclusion about the nucleus did this support?
options: The nucleus is negatively charged and attracts alpha particles
The nucleus is positively charged and repels alpha particles
The nucleus is made of neutrons
markScheme: 1 mark: The nucleus is positively charged and repels alpha particles
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are positive. The way they were pushed away from the centre shows that the nucleus is positive and repels them. A neutral nucleus would not deflect them by electrostatic force.

questions.question: Why was it important that the gold foil in the scattering experiment was very thin?
options: So that alpha particles passed through only a few layers of atoms
So that the foil did not become radioactive
So that electrons could escape from the foil
So that the foil would not melt
markScheme: 1 mark: So that alpha particles passed through only a few layers of atoms
questions.explanation: A very thin foil means each alpha particle interacts with only a few atoms, so deflections can be linked to single nuclei. Thick foil would absorb the alpha particles.

questions.question: Name the subatomic particle whose discovery led to the plum pudding model.
markScheme: 1 mark: electron
questions.explanation: Finding electrons showed atoms could be divided, so a new model was needed.

questions.question: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
markScheme: 1 mark: a ball (sphere) of positive charge
1 mark: with negative electrons embedded in it
questions.explanation: Both the positive ball and the embedded electrons are needed for full marks.

questions.question: State two differences between the plum pudding model and the nuclear model.
acceptedAnswers: positive charge spread out vs concentrated in nucleus
mass spread out vs concentrated in nucleus
markScheme: 1 mark: plum pudding has positive charge spread throughout; nuclear model has positive charge concentrated in a tiny nucleus
1 mark: plum pudding has mass spread out; nuclear model has mass concentrated in the nucleus / nuclear model is mostly empty space / electrons outside the nucleus
questions.explanation: Each difference should state both models. Positive charge, mass and empty space are the key ideas.

questions.question: Describe the three main observations from the alpha particle scattering experiment.
markScheme: 1 mark: most alpha particles passed straight through
1 mark: some were deflected (through small angles)
1 mark: a very small number bounced back (deflected through more than 90°)
questions.explanation: Use quantity words carefully: most, some, very few.

questions.question: Explain what the observation that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil tells us about atoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: most of the atom is empty space
1 mark: so most alpha particles did not come close to the (tiny) nucleus
questions.explanation: If the atom were solid, alpha particles would not get through. Passing straight through means they met nothing.

questions.question: Explain why Bohr's model of the atom was accepted by other scientists.
markScheme: 1 mark: his theoretical calculations (predictions)
1 mark: agreed with experimental observations
questions.explanation: A model gains acceptance when its predictions match what is measured.

questions.question: Describe what later experiments showed about the positive charge of a nucleus.
markScheme: 1 mark: the positive charge could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles
1 mark: each with the same amount of positive charge (protons)
questions.explanation: This is how protons were identified as the units of nuclear charge.

questions.question: Suggest why neutrons were discovered much later than protons and electrons.
markScheme: 1 mark: neutrons have no charge
1 mark: so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields / do not ionise, making them hard to detect
questions.explanation: Charged particles are easy to detect by their effects. Neutral particles leave little trace, so evidence took longer to find.

questions.question: State what was fired at the gold foil in the scattering experiment.
markScheme: 1 mark: alpha particles
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are positive, which is why the deflections revealed a positive nucleus.

questions.question: Name the model of the atom that replaced the plum pudding model.
markScheme: 1 mark: nuclear model
questions.explanation: The nuclear model has a small, dense, positive nucleus.

questions.question: What charge do alpha particles have?
markScheme: 1 mark: Positive
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are two protons and two neutrons, so they are positive. This is why they are repelled by the positive nucleus.

questions.question: Explain why the plum pudding model predicts that alpha particles fired at gold foil should all pass through with very little deflection.
markScheme: 1 mark: positive charge (and mass) is spread out through the atom
1 mark: so the electric force on an alpha particle is small / cancels
1 mark: so there is nothing able to cause large deflections or bounce particles back
questions.explanation: With charge spread thinly, no region could exert a large repulsive force, so the large-angle scattering was a surprise.

questions.question: Which observation from the alpha scattering experiment most clearly could NOT be explained by the plum pudding model?
options: Most alpha particles passed straight through
The gold foil was not damaged
A few alpha particles bounced back
Alpha particles travelled in straight lines in air
markScheme: 1 mark: A few alpha particles bounced back
questions.explanation: The plum pudding model predicts alpha particles passing through, so straight-through results fit it. Bouncing back needs a concentrated, massive charge, which plum pudding does not have.

questions.question: Which part of the atom did the alpha scattering experiment reveal?
markScheme: 1 mark: The nucleus
questions.explanation: Alpha scattering showed that the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. Electrons were already known, and neutrons and energy levels came later.

questions.question: Describe how the model of the atom changed from the idea of indivisible spheres to the nuclear model. Refer to the evidence that caused each change.
markScheme: Indicative content: atoms first thought to be tiny indivisible spheres; discovery of the electron showed atoms contain smaller charged particles; this led to the plum pudding model, a ball of positive charge with electrons embedded; alpha scattering experiment fired alpha particles at gold foil; most passed through, some deflected, few bounced back; showed mass concentrated in a small positive nucleus; nuclear model replaced plum pudding.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear sequence linking each model change to the evidence.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some models named or described with little link to evidence.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key is linking each change to new evidence: electron discovery, then alpha scattering.

questions.question: Describe the alpha particle scattering experiment and explain how its results led scientists to replace the plum pudding model. Include how the nuclear model was later developed by Bohr and Chadwick.
markScheme: Indicative content: positive alpha particles fired at very thin gold foil; detector placed at different angles; most passed straight through, so atom mostly empty space; some deflected, so nucleus charged (positive, repels alpha particles); very few bounced back, so mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus; plum pudding model has spread-out charge and mass so cannot explain large deflections; nuclear model replaced it; Bohr suggested electrons orbit at specific distances and his calculations agreed with experiments; later the positive charge was found to be made of protons; Chadwick provided evidence for neutrons about 20 years after the nucleus was accepted.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logical account linking all three observations to conclusions, explaining the failure of the plum pudding model, and describing Bohr's and Chadwick's contributions.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): observations and some conclusions given, with partial explanation or limited reference to later developments.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about the experiment or models with little linking.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers pair every observation with a conclusion, then explain why plum pudding fails and outline the later refinements in the right order.
